draft.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
card: Parallel lines never meet. They have equal gradients, so \(y = 3x + 1\) and \(y = 3x - 4\) are parallel.
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. Their gradients multiply to \(-1\).
To find a perpendicular gradient, flip the fraction and change the sign. The gradient \(2\) is \(\frac{2}{1}\), so a perpendicular line has gradient \(-\frac{1}{2}\).
Example: a line has gradient \(-\frac{3}{4}\). Flip it to get \(\frac{4}{3}\), then change the sign. The perpendicular gradient is \(\frac{4}{3}\). Check: \(-\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{4}{3} = -1\).
draft.remember: Parallel: same gradient. Perpendicular: flip it and change the sign.

a.why: The gradient of the given line is \(5\). The perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{1}{5}\), because \(5 \times -\frac{1}{5} = -1\). The line \(y = \frac{1}{5}x + 2\) only flips the fraction and keeps the sign, so its product with \(5\) is \(1\), not \(-1\).
a.clue: Flip the gradient, then change its sign.

b.q: Line \(p\) has equation \(y = -\frac{2}{3}x + 7\). Line \(q\) is perpendicular to \(p\). What is the gradient of \(q\)?
b.why: The gradient of \(p\) is \(-\frac{2}{3}\). Flip it to get \(\frac{3}{2}\) and change the sign, which gives \(\frac{3}{2}\). Check: \(-\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{2} = -1\). The option \(-\frac{3}{2}\) flips the fraction but forgets to change the sign.
b.clue: The original gradient is negative, so the new one must be positive.

problems.detail: The worked example says flipping \(-\frac{3}{4}\) gives \(\frac{4}{3}\), then changing the sign gives \(\frac{4}{3}\). Flipping gives \(-\frac{4}{3}\), and changing the sign then gives \(\frac{4}{3}\). As written, 'change the sign' leaves the number unchanged, which contradicts the rule just taught and will confuse students.

The why repeats the card's error: 'Flip it to get \(\frac{3}{2}\) and change the sign, which gives \(\frac{3}{2}\).' Flipping \(-\frac{2}{3}\) gives \(-\frac{3}{2}\), and changing the sign gives \(\frac{3}{2}\). The why's own later sentence, that \(-\frac{3}{2}\) flips but forgets the sign change, contradicts its first step.

check.summary: Both answers are right (\(y = -\frac{1}{5}x + 2\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\)). The card's worked example and why (b) both mis-state the flip step: they drop the negative sign when flipping, so 'change the sign' appears to do nothing. Fix: flipping \(-\frac{3}{4}\) gives \(-\frac{4}{3}\), and flipping \(-\frac{2}{3}\) gives \(-\frac{3}{2}\).
